rule_name: 4. Invented similes versus inherited similes
quote: the way you'd read it off a card you'd written in the car
why: a newly built, writerly comparison placed in narration rather than a character's mouth, matching the banned pattern of 'the way you'd put something down'
suggestion: her mom says, and she has the whole list ready in order, each item already decided before she walked in

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: writes for a second
why: 'for a second' is used as a generic universal duration marker rather than a real, specific measure of the moment
suggestion: Dr. Ammons writes a line before she asks the next one

rule_name: 8. Automatic-fail narrator constructions (Anaphora / three-beat lists)
quote: Whether the same adults were there the whole four weeks. Whether anything happened. Whether Chloe came back different, and in what way, and starting when.
why: three consecutive 'Whether' sentence fragments in narration is the banned anaphora pattern the rule names outright
suggestion: whether the same adults were there the whole four weeks, whether anything happened, whether Chloe came back different, and in what way, and starting when

rule_name: Banned Constructions, Assert Nothing, Show the Substance
quote: it was the best month she's ever had
why: a bare ranking verdict with no supporting fact, a close variant of the banned 'that is the best' family
suggestion: she asked to go back the day we picked her up, and hasn't stopped since

rule_name: Thought Reported vs. Thought Rendered
quote: Chloe thinks about it for a while
why: states the fact of thinking rather than rendering it, almost verbatim the rule's own banned example 'she thought about that one for a while'
suggestion: cut the clause and open straight on the list: 'There are about forty things and they won't go in a line: the bridge going over sideways all at once...'

rule_name: 8. Automatic-fail narrator constructions (Superlatives in narration)
quote: never once mentioning that he was doing it
why: 'never once' is a banned narrator superlative; the rule allows it only in dialogue, and this is narration
suggestion: There's Mr. Baptiste doing the whole rectangle over from the beginning for Marisol, not mentioning it

rule_name: 5. The trailing clause
quote: the way she does when there's a thing to say first
why: the sentence is complete before the comma; the tail exists only to tell the reader how to read the gesture
suggestion: In the car her mom holds the wheel with both hands without starting the engine.

rule_name: Filtering, Cut "She Sees / Hears / Notices / Knows"
quote: she watches the wall of the building start to slide sideways past her window
why: routes the image through the perception verb 'watches' instead of rendering the motion directly
suggestion: the wall of the building slides sideways past her window

rule_name: 8. Automatic-fail narrator constructions (Interiority of non-POV characters)
quote: which everyone in the building appears to be pleased with themselves about
why: attributes an internal emotional state to unnamed school staff who are not Chloe, something narration is not entitled to know
suggestion: cut the clause, or give an observable detail: 'which the woman on the phone says twice, like it's good news'

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: spending a while getting nine people out of four different classrooms
why: 'a while' is used as a generic universal duration marker rather than a specific one
suggestion: spending ten minutes getting nine people out of four different classrooms

rule_name: Vague Abstractions, Replace "Something," "Nothing," "The Whole Thing"
quote: because there is nothing after the twelfth one
why: 'nothing' stands in as emotional shorthand for the letdown of running out of problems, almost identical to the rule's own banned example about the worksheet
suggestion: because the twelfth one is the last one, and after that there's only the clock

rule_name: 5. The trailing clause
quote: the way she was taught to expect by four weeks of things turning
why: the sentence is complete before the comma; the tail explains the preceding statement instead of adding a fact, and the next two sentences already do the explaining
suggestion: She keeps waiting for it to turn. At camp there was a point in every single thing where it stopped being easy...

rule_name: 4. Invented similes versus inherited similes
quote: the way people smile when they think you have said something sweet
why: a newly built, writerly comparison in narration rather than a character's mouth
suggestion: Mrs. Prahl smiles at her, indulgent, and doesn't answer the question

rule_name: Banned Constructions, Assert Nothing, Show the Substance
quote: That's not true and you know perfectly well it isn't true.
why: the entire sentence is a bare verdict on truth-value with no fact offered, a close variant of the banned 'that's wrong' / 'I was wrong' family
suggestion: "Dad and I have both said no every time you've asked. That's not the same as hating you."

rule_name: Vague Abstractions, Replace "Something," "Nothing," "The Whole Thing"
quote: Her mom's face does something
why: 'does something' is a vague placeholder standing in for an actual, nameable change in her mother's expression
suggestion: Her mom's mouth goes tight at the corner

rule_name: Filtering, Cut "She Sees / Hears / Notices / Knows"
quote: which Chloe sees it do from about four feet away
why: routes the observation through the filter verb 'sees' instead of rendering the expression directly
suggestion: from about four feet away, and she doesn't stop for it

rule_name: The "Nobody" Construction, Don't Normalise by Reporting an Absent Reaction
quote: Nobody comes up.
why: reports an absent reaction as evidence that no one is coming to check on her, the exact banned pattern the rule names
suggestion: give a specific detail instead: 'The television keeps going downstairs.'

rule_name: Repetition as Emphasis, Say It Once and Let Placement Do the Work
quote: She waits there a long time and nobody comes up.
why: restates 'nobody comes up' one sentence after saying it, with no new information added by the repeat
suggestion: She waits there a long time, until her legs ache from standing behind the door.

rule_name: 8. Automatic-fail narrator constructions (Narrator evaluation / ranking)
quote: her mother is completely normal to her
why: the narrator supplies the evaluative label 'normal' before the concrete evidence (bread, milk, the Thursday question) instead of letting the details earn the conclusion
suggestion: cut the label and open directly on the evidence: 'At dinner her mother passes her the bread, asks whether she wants more milk...'

rule_name: The "Nobody" Construction, Don't Normalise by Reporting an Absent Reaction
quote: Neither of them says one word about any of it, then or afterward.
why: reports an absent reaction (no one mentioning the fight) as evidence of the household's avoidance, the banned 'nobody' pattern in a 'neither' variant
suggestion: give one specific detail instead: 'Her dad passes the salt before she asks for it.'

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: a thing with the dice
why: 'a thing' is a vague placeholder for an unnamed activity, matching the banned 'the thing where' family
suggestion: for a dice-probability game

rule_name: Subordinate Instead of Chaining With "And" / "Then"
quote: because it's faster than her class, and everybody keeps telling her it's the fast one, and Mrs. Prahl is nice to her every single week, and there are nine of them in that room instead of twenty-six
why: four distinct, differently weighted reasons are coordinated with 'and' instead of subordinated, so the sentence can't distinguish which fact carries the most weight
suggestion: because, faster than her class as it is, with everybody calling it the fast one and Mrs. Prahl nice to her every week, there are still only nine of them in that room instead of twenty-six

rule_name: 3. Reification and the grep test
quote: goes looking for it, and finds it right there at the front where she doesn't have to reach for it
why: hands an abstraction (the answer to her mother's question) a physical verb, treating it as an object she can search for, locate, and reach for
suggestion: Chloe sits up and answers straight away, without having to think about it. It's one thing, and it's small.

rule_name: Vague Abstractions, Replace "Something," "Nothing," "The Whole Thing"
quote: nothing happening to her
why: 'nothing' stands in as vague shorthand for a specific, meaningful absence instead of naming what didn't happen
suggestion: and no one's hand landing on her, the whole four weeks

rule_name: Emotional Detachment, Render the Physical Correlate, Not the Label
quote: her hands still cold
why: 'cold hands' is named directly in the rule as a physiological cliché that could describe any anxious character in any scene
suggestion: standing there afterward with the hallway tile cold enough through her socks to notice

rule_name: Keep Narrative Tense Consistent Unless the Break Is Signalled
quote: which Chloe knew about by the second week of December and never said anything about to anybody
why: an unsignalled dip into simple past inside a chapter told consistently in present tense everywhere else
suggestion: which Chloe knows about by the second week of December and never says anything about to anybody

rule_name: Ration a Character's Verbal Tic to the Moments It Characterises
quote: there are nine people standing around the front room
why: the manuscript's exact-count tic (echoing the rule's own examples like 'ninety seconds') is applied here to an ordinary Christmas moment with no anxiety, control, or dissociation at stake, so it reads as narrator autopilot rather than characterisation
suggestion: there are people standing around the front room in their coats watching her see it

rule_name: Ration a Character's Verbal Tic to the Moments It Characterises
quote: there are eleven people in the house and Chloe knows all of them
why: the exact-count tic is used again for an ordinary family gathering with no tension attached, the default use the rule warns against
suggestion: there are more people in the house than Chloe can keep track of, and she knows all of them anyway

rule_name: 8. Automatic-fail narrator constructions (Stacked negatives)
quote: She doesn't decide to stop, or notice herself stopping, or say anything to anybody about it.
why: three negatives stacked in one sentence, the exact pattern the rule tells you to restate as one positive statement
suggestion: It happens without her, somewhere in the last week of January.

rule_name: Filtering, Cut "She Sees / Hears / Notices / Knows"
quote: She notices at the end of the month
why: routes the realization through the filter verb 'notices' instead of rendering it directly
suggestion: At the end of the month, standing at the sink brushing her teeth, it's been days since she asked

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: she hasn't asked in a while
why: 'a while' is a generic universal duration marker instead of a real one
suggestion: she hasn't asked in eleven days

rule_name: The "Nobody" Construction, Don't Normalise by Reporting an Absent Reaction
quote: nobody in the house has said one word about her not asking
why: reports an absent reaction as proof the household has normalised her silence, the banned 'nobody' pattern
suggestion: and the strawberry magnet on the fridge is holding up a grocery list now instead of the note

rule_name: 8. Automatic-fail narrator constructions (Narrator evaluation / Interiority of non-POV characters)
quote: Her parents are relieved
why: states a conclusion about both parents' internal state as settled fact before any evidence, attributing interiority to her dad, a non-POV character whose feelings Chloe can only infer from what she overhears
suggestion: cut the label and start on the evidence: 'She hears it from the stairs on a Sunday, her mom saying she thinks the Thursdays are helping...'

rule_name: Vague Abstractions, Replace "Something," "Nothing," "The Whole Thing"
quote: There's nothing to do with it.
why: 'nothing' closes the chapter on vague emotional shorthand instead of a specific, nameable action or feeling
suggestion: She doesn't open it again after that.
